description: Equipo de desarrolladores que construye una herramienta con datos de NASA para ayudar a agricultores de Guatemala a tomar mejores decisiones
summary: Milpa Resiliente turns two decades of satellite records into a three-fact traffic light for smallholder farmers in Guatemala's Dry Corridor: months with bare soil or little cover around the plot (NASA MODIS NDVI), years with fire detected nearby (NASA FIRMS VIIRS) and years with a long mid-summer dry spell, the canícula (CHIRPS v3 with NASA GPM IMERG). Each fact has a shape, a word, a pictogram and a short audio in Spanish or English. One tap away, an Evidence view lets the extension worker compare three crop rotations per plot, today and in 33 to 34 NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate futures for 2041-2060, with sources, validation and limits. It matters: for July-September 2026, 3.2 million Guatemalans (17 %) were forecast in food crisis or worse, and FEWS NET reported maize losses, in some cases total, in the Dry Corridor. The tool does not decide: it gives the farmer and the extension worker the same evidence. A farmer who tried it during a remote visit says it looks good; longer use in the field and without signal comes next.
details:
What it does. Milpa Resiliente is a static website for five example plots in Chiquimula and Zacapa (Jocotán, Camotán, Olopa, San Juan Ermita and Zacapa). It has two views and works in English and Spanish.

  • Farmer view (first screen). Three facts the satellite saw around the plot, always in the same order: bare soil, fire near the plot and long canícula. Each fact gets one of four states: green circle “Good”, yellow triangle “Watch out”, red square “Happens often”, or gray “The satellite can't see well here” when a source has no data. The view avoids orange and the word “alert”, so it is not mistaken for CONRED's public alert levels (green, yellow, orange and red); every state also carries a shape and a word, so it never relies on colour. Pictograms show the quantities: a 12-month wheel for bare soil and one dot per year for fire and dry spells. Each fact also says, in plain words, what happened, when and how often (for example, “In March and April, your land is usually left with no plants covering it”). Two more cards follow: this year's July-August rain against a normal year and the driest year since 1991 (preliminary), and each crop option in NASA's 33 climate futures for 2041-2060, drawn as 33 plants that stay green or dry up. Below, the options to talk over with the extension worker: the current practice, the best legume or cover-crop option and the best drought-tolerant option. Options within 3 points of one another are shown as even, in no order, instead of naming a winner; the rule works as a chain, so in Olopa (87, 90 and 92) all three count as even. A Listen button reads the same sentences aloud, about a minute or less, with subtitles, in Spanish or English to match the screen; the voice is synthetic.
  • Evidence view (one tap away). For the extension worker: a map with NASA GIBS true-colour layers stored in the site for offline use, plus Sentinel-2 imagery when there is a connection, what the satellite sees, the climate of the area, the three rotations side by side with water, soil and pest scores and a 12-month calendar, rainfall scenarios of 0, −10, −20 and −30 % with +1.5 °C, the three rotations tested in each NASA climate future for 2041-2060 (one dot per model), a printable farmer card, a “NASA product → decision” table, a “Where it fails” panel, the validation and every source.

How it works. A Python pipeline downloads and caches the data for each plot, recording its URL, date, product and version. A rules engine in plain Python (standard library plus PyYAML) detects bare-soil months, fires and dry spells, runs an FAO-56 water balance with yield response factors, scores the rotations and writes one JSON file per plot that follows a JSON schema. The web (React, Leaflet, Recharts, built with Vite) reads only those files, so it needs no server and no keys. Texts in both languages come from deterministic templates, and a validator rejects any number that is not in the engine's JSON and any planting date that does not come from ZARC (FAO–MAGA). Planting dates are quoted, never calculated.

Local roots. The cover and no-burn option follows the principles of Kuxur Rum (“my humid land” in Ch'orti'), an agroforestry system that FAO and Guatemala's Ministry of Agriculture have promoted in Chiquimula since 2000: permanent soil cover, no burning and more soil moisture through the canícula, the same three things the traffic light tracks. By 2006 more than 7,000 farms had adopted it. Jocotán, Camotán and Olopa are Ch'orti' Maya territory, and 112,432 people speak Ch'orti'. The data contract already reserves an audio slot for Ch'orti', and the repository includes the phrase script ready for native speakers to translate and record (docs/chorti.md). We did not machine-translate or synthesise Ch'orti': without review by speakers it could be wrong and disrespectful.

How we test the rotations against the future. In Google Earth Engine we took NASA's NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 daily projections (0.25°, bias-corrected) for each plot: May-October rain, June-August rain (the canícula) and mean temperature, for 2041-2060 against 1995-2014, in every model available (33 under SSP2-4.5 and 34 under SSP5-8.5). Each model is compared only with its own past, so its bias cancels out. The engine applies each model's change to the observed daily series and reruns the same water balance for the three rotations. A rotation "holds" in a future when its water score is equal to or higher than today's practice with today's climate. Earth Engine is used only offline to precompute the cache; the website never calls it. The median model projects 4 % less May-October rain, 7 % less June-August rain and +1.4 °C under SSP2-4.5, and 12 % less, 17 % less and +2.1 °C under SSP5-8.5. 23 to 24 of 33 models (SSP2-4.5) and 29 to 30 of 34 (SSP5-8.5) project less rain than today.

How we checked it. We fixed the rule before looking at the result: no threshold is tuned to make 2018 come out right. Using only data up to 2017 (water deficit with CHIRPS rain; SMAP is not part of this run), the engine flags 2018 as high risk at 5 of 5 plots. FAO GIEWS relayed a preliminary MAGA estimate of 175,126 ha of crop losses, mainly maize and beans, in Guatemala as of 13 August 2018. One year and five points are a sanity check, not a skill score, so we also count the misses. Over the 20 test years (2006-2025) the same rule flags 5 or 6 years per plot. Against the four dry years we had listed (2014, 2015, 2018, 2019) it hits 3, with 2 or 3 false alarms and 1 miss. Against seven years with publicly documented crop losses (2009, 2010, 2015, 2016, 2018, 2019, 2023) it hits 3 or 4 and misses 2016, 2019 and 2023 at every plot. We also measured where NASA POWER's default rainfall (about 50 km) fails at this scale (from −22 % to +55 % in July-August against CHIRPS) and used CHIRPS for rain instead; POWER now also offers IMERG rainfall at 0.1°, which we have not tested. Separately, the site shows a preliminary observation, not a forecast: in CHIRPS v3, the five plots' cells got 20 % to 26 % of their 1991-2025 median July-August rainfall in 2026, the lowest since 1991. FEWS NET reported 5 % to 25 % of normal August rainfall across the Dry Corridor, but its map uses the same Climate Hazards Center data, so it is consistent rather than independent.

Benefits. The farmer sees what satellites recorded around their own plot, in a form designed to work without reading well and to print in black and white; a real photocopy is still pending. In a remote visit on 15 November, a farmer who used the app once or twice said it looks good, and the farmer view worked with TalkBack, Android's screen reader, on a real phone. The extension worker gets the evidence, the confidence level and its reason for each option. The site is built to keep working without internet: an automated test with the network blocked passes, but it still needs longer use in the field. Every claim links to its source and its limits.

Limits we state openly. The five points were chosen from NDVI and Sentinel-2 imagery and visited only remotely (15 November), not yet in person. A Dry Corridor family farms about 0.35 ha on average, while one MODIS pixel covers 6.25 ha, a SMAP cell 9 km and an SRTM cell 90 m: the tool describes the land around the plot, not the plot. An agronomist confirmed three facts we rely on (ICTA B-7 is the most used maize in eastern Guatemala because of its drought tolerance, postrera beans are planted in August and September, and 10 days without rain at flowering already damage maize), but has not reviewed the scoring rules yet, and the traffic-light cut-offs were set after seeing the five plots' counts. The climate futures change mean rain and temperature, not the number of rainy days; Jocotán, Camotán and San Juan Ermita share one 0.25° NASA cell, so they share the projected change; and the drought-tolerant option starts with a higher water score, which favours it in the count. A first pictogram test with three adults who are not farmers found that 1 of 3 read every drawing without help, and 2 of 3 also read the canícula sun as good weather; a test with farmers is still pending. Camotán has no SMAP data of recommended quality. Suomi NPP stopped delivering new data in early November 2026 and Terra is being retired, so updates would move to VIIRS on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. This is not an early-warning system and it does not replace ZARC, MAGA, INSIVUMEH or CONRED: it complements ZARC and the Agroclimatic Technical Boards (docs/existing-tools.md).

Tools. Python 3.11, PyYAML, requests, pytest and jsonschema; Google Earth Engine Code Editor (offline precompute only); JavaScript with React, Leaflet (react-leaflet), Recharts and Vite; edge-tts for the voice; a Windows laptop. No paid services.

Use of AI (Super Intelligence). An AI coding agent (Claude, by Anthropic) wrote most of the code, most of the texts in both languages and the SVG code of the pictograms, always under the team's direction and review. The same agent wrote the Earth Engine script and the module that tests the rotations in each NASA climate future. A research agent with web search found the agronomic sources and, on 14 November, the impact figures and the status of each sensor; every figure we use carries its URL, we checked every quote against its document, and the ones that could not be confirmed were left out. Before building, an AI assistant compared this idea with five others; the team chose. The team decided the scope, the five plots, the traffic-light thresholds, the tie rule and the validation rule. The audio uses synthetic voices (edge-tts: es-GT-MartaNeural and en-US-JennyNeural), labelled as AI-generated next to the player and in each mp3's tags. The 30-second demo video was assembled by the same AI coding agent with HyperFrames (HTML rendered to video) from real screens of the site and our data; its narration is a synthetic ElevenLabs voice, labelled on the end card. No AI produces any number the user sees: numbers come from the data and from rules in code, and texts come from fixed templates checked by a validator that rejects any number that is not in the engine's output. Full declaration: docs/ai-use.md in the repository.
